title: Check for Student Understanding: Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction [FREE GUIDE & RESOURCE]
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Clark presents checking for understanding as real-time diagnosis: asking every student to show their thinking so the teacher can adjust immediately, rather than asking whether there are any questions. She quotes Rosenshine's contrast between effective teachers who checked frequently and ineffective ones who assumed silence meant learning. Checks matter because they expose the illusion of learning, move new material toward long-term memory, and allow responsive teaching through low-stakes feedback loops. Drawing on a Carl Hendrick and Haili Hughes webinar, she frames CfU as a planned sequence of decisions about when, how, who and what next. Her operating rule is to keep checks diagnostic and inclusive, then act: reteach if fewer than about 80% have it. The step-by-step routine and some resources are behind the paywall.
points: Asking Are there any questions is not a check; effective checking requires every student to show what they understand.
CfU is diagnostic rather than summative, and its value lies in the teacher's next move, reteaching or extending based on the evidence.
Frequent checks expose the illusion of learning and help consolidate new material into long-term memory.
Inclusive formats like mini-whiteboards, cold call with wait-time and think-pair-share keep students from slipping under the radar.
quotes: CfU is the ongoing process of asking students to show you their thinking so you can adjust teaching immediately. Rather than asking “Does that make sense?” or “Who can tell me the answer?” you ask targeted questions so every student demonstrates what they’ve understood.

The more effective teachers frequently checked to see if all the students were learning the new material… In contrast, the less effective teachers simply asked, ‘Are there any questions?’ and, if there were no questions, they assumed the students had learned the material and proceeded to pass out worksheets…

Think of CfU as a bridge between teaching and learning: it’s not about testing for a grade but about giving you and your students a clear picture of what’s secure, what’s shaky, and what needs reteaching right now.

Done well, CfU moments make learning more visible and more equitable — especially for students who might otherwise slip under the radar. What’s more, Rosenshine explains that checks are important for consolidating learning and transferring new information into long-term memory.
These checks provided some of the processing needed to move new learning into long-term memory. These checks also let teachers know if students were developing misconceptions.
Plan how you’ll respond to what you see. If less than ~80 % grasp it, reteach or adjust; if most have it, extend or deepen.
